issues.legal_issue: An application styled as one for clarification, modification, or recall cannot be used to bypass the prescribed circulation procedure when it is in substance a review application.
material_facts: After a review petition had been dismissed, the applicant filed applications seeking, among other things, recall or modification of the original judgment and relief on grounds that substantially repeated the review grounds.
The applications sought an open-court hearing despite the rule that review applications are ordinarily considered in circulation.
issues.conclusion: An application that is in substance a review cannot obtain an open-court hearing merely by being described as an application for clarification, modification, or recall. The court may reject it, with or without costs, or permit its withdrawal with leave to file a review application for consideration in circulation; a second review is not permitted after disposal of the first.
issues.legal_principle: Order XL Rules 1, 3, and 5 of the Supreme Court Rules, 1966, restrict review to the specified grounds, provide for disposal by circulation unless otherwise ordered, and bar a further review after disposal of a review application. A review is not an appeal in disguise: Thungabhara Industries Ltd. v. Government of Andhra Pradesh. The court also referred to Sonelal v. State of U.P. in deprecating attempts to evade the review procedure.

rule.if: post_judgment_application and (review_already_dismissed or application_seeks_review_relief) and application_is_review_in_substance

predicates.post_judgment_application: A party filed an application after the court had finally decided the matter.
predicates.review_already_dismissed: The court had already disposed of a review application in the same matter.
predicates.application_seeks_review_relief: The application seeks to change or undo the substance of the court's earlier decision.
predicates.application_is_review_in_substance: The application raises grounds for reconsidering the earlier decision rather than seeking a genuinely necessary clarification or procedural correction.

issues.definition: When a post-judgment application seeks reconsideration in substance, it is not entitled to an open-court hearing through a label other than review, including where a review has already been dismissed.

issues.legal_issue: A later reasoned order explaining an operative order that made a rule absolute cannot extend the relief beyond the scope of that operative order.
material_facts: A High Court first made the rule absolute in a set of individual land-acquisition writ petitions by an operative order, with reasons to follow.
The later reasoned order made broad observations about defects in the inquiry and declaration, but the objections at issue were personal to individual landowners.

The Supreme Court's earlier three-judge decision had confined the effect of the High Court orders to the petitions and land covered by the operative orders, and the two-judge decision under review had followed that ruling rather than an earlier decision that had not considered the operative orders.
issues.conclusion: The later reasoned order could not enlarge the relief beyond the operative orders in the individual writ petitions. The three-judge ruling had been correctly decided and followed, and no reference to a larger Bench was warranted.
issues.legal_principle: The operative order controls the scope of relief when reasons are supplied later; the reasons cannot travel beyond the four corners of the order already made. The court held that Abhey Ram v. Union of India correctly confined the effect of the High Court's operative orders and explained and distinguished Delhi Development Authority v. Sudan Singh. It also held that a decision operating between particular parties does not, merely through broad language in later reasons, determine the rights of persons whose cases were not before the court.

predicates.land_acquisition_case: The proceeding concerns the validity or effect of land-acquisition proceedings.
predicates.operative_order_limited_to_individual_pe: The court's operative order made the rule absolute in specified individual petitions rather than granting relief in a proceeding covering all affected landowners.
predicates.later_reasons_address_personal_objection: The reasons supplied later discuss defects concerning objections particular to individual landowners rather than a defect going to the root of the acquisition for everyone.

issues.definition: In a land-acquisition case, when the operative order grants relief in individual petitions and later reasons address personal objections, those reasons do not extend the relief beyond the operative order.

issues.legal_issue: A declaration that land is needed for a public purpose need not itself give detailed reasons or address each parcel individually when the Government has considered the inquiry report.
material_facts: The landowner challenged the declaration on the ground that the Government had not shown its application of mind through detailed reasons in the declaration.
The declaration recorded that the Government had considered the inquiry report and objections and was satisfied that the land was needed for a public purpose.
The Government's consideration of the inquiry report and the basis for its satisfaction could be examined from the record if challenged.
issues.conclusion: The declaration need not state reasons or refer to objections concerning every parcel. If the Government's satisfaction is challenged, it may justify that satisfaction by producing the record on which it acted.
issues.legal_principle: Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 requires the Government's satisfaction that land is needed for a public purpose but does not require the declaration to set out detailed reasons for each parcel. The court relied on Ganga Bishnu v. Cal Pinjrapole Society, which held that the declaration need not itself recite the satisfaction if it is made in the prescribed manner and that the record can prove the satisfaction, and Ratilal Shakarabhai v. State of Gujarat, which rejected a challenge alleging that the Government acted blindly after examining the inquiry report.

predicates.land_acquisition_case: The proceeding concerns a declaration made in a land-acquisition process.
predicates.declaration_follows_consideration_of_inq: The Government issued the declaration after considering the report of the inquiry into objections.
predicates.challenge_claims_declaration_lacks_indiv: A challenger alleges that the declaration is invalid because it does not state detailed reasons or address each parcel separately.

issues.definition: Where a land-acquisition declaration follows consideration of the inquiry report, the absence of individual reasons in the declaration does not by itself invalidate it.

issues.legal_issue: A landowner who did not object during the statutory inquiry cannot later challenge the acquisition on personal grounds that could have been raised there, but may still challenge whether the acquisition serves a public purpose.
material_facts: The landowner had not filed objections during the inquiry into objections to the proposed acquisition.
The challenge relied on matters personal to the landowner or the land, including whether the land was necessary or should be excluded in light of particular circumstances.
The existence of a public purpose was not disputed in the case.
issues.conclusion: Personal grounds that could have been raised in the inquiry were deemed waived, and the landowner could not use them to challenge the inquiry or declaration. The failure to object does not prevent a challenge to whether the acquisition is for a public purpose.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 5A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, objections may concern the existence of a public purpose or matters personal to the land or objector. A person who does not raise personal objections is deemed to have waived them and cannot later challenge the Section 5A inquiry or Section 6 declaration on those grounds. The court applied the principle stated in Abhey Ram v. Union of India, while recognizing that the public-purpose objection remains available even if no objections were filed.

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: The proceeding challenges the validity of land-acquisition proceedings.
predicates.no_objections_submitted: The affected landowner did not submit objections during the statutory inquiry into the proposed acquisition.
predicates.challenge_rests_on_personal_or_land_spec: The challenge concerns the landowner's individual circumstances or the suitability or necessity of acquiring that particular land.

issues.definition: When a landowner raises no objections during the inquiry, a later challenge on personal or land-specific grounds is unavailable, while a challenge to the existence of a public purpose remains available.

issues.legal_issue: A landowner who relied on an authority's representation that acquisition proceedings had been quashed may be given an opportunity to have a release request considered, subject to the stated eligibility conditions and the authority's discretion.
material_facts: An authority had represented to the applicant that the acquisition proceedings had been quashed and directed the applicant to seek approval for construction.
The applicant relied on that representation and constructed a building after obtaining approval of the building plans.

The Government's counsel accepted that a release request could be considered if the applicant was the original owner before the acquisition notification, the construction complied with the approved plans and applicable building limits, and compensation had not been paid.
The court did not order release of the land; it directed consideration of a timely application and left the extent of any release to the competent authority's reasonable discretion.
issues.conclusion: The applicant's request for release was to be considered in light of the representation, the stated conditions, and the relevant circumstances, with a reasoned decision communicated to the applicant. The extent of any release was left to the competent authority's discretion.
issues.legal_principle: Section 48 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 permits withdrawal from acquisition in the circumstances provided by that provision. The court noted that the authority's representation, acted upon by the applicant, raised a prima facie question of estoppel under Section 115 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, and gave effect to the Government's concession by directing consideration of a release request rather than ordering release.

rule.if: land_acquisition_case and authority_represented_acquisition_was_quashed and applicant_relied_on_representation_to_build and applicant_was_original_owner and construction_was_approved_and_plan_compliant and compensation_unpaid and release_application_submitted

predicates.land_acquisition_case: The proceeding concerns land subject to acquisition proceedings.
predicates.authority_represented_acquisition_was_qu: An authority told the applicant that the acquisition proceedings affecting the land had been quashed.
predicates.applicant_relied_on_representation_to_bu: The applicant relied on the authority's representation in constructing a building on the land.
predicates.applicant_was_original_owner: The applicant owned the land before the acquisition process began and was not merely a later transferee.
predicates.construction_was_approved_and_plan_compl: The building plans were approved and the construction complied with those plans and applicable building limits.
predicates.compensation_unpaid: Compensation for the acquired land had not been paid.
predicates.release_application_submitted: The applicant submitted a request seeking release of the land from acquisition.

issues.definition: When the stated representation, reliance, ownership, construction, compensation, and application facts are present, the release request must be considered and decided by a reasoned decision, while the extent of any release remains discretionary.

issues.legal_issue: A constitutional writ challenging a later administrative direction may be dismissed with liberty to raise the disputed contentions before the High Court without the Supreme Court deciding their merits.
material_facts: A petitioner brought a constitutional writ challenging a later administrative direction concerning land affected by acquisition proceedings.
The respondents disputed the petitioner's ownership and raised other legal and factual issues concerning the land and the asserted effect of related documents.
The Supreme Court considered it appropriate for the petitioner to raise the contentions before the High Court and expressly left their merits open.
issues.conclusion: The writ petition was dismissed, with liberty for the petitioner to move the High Court; the Supreme Court expressed no view on the merits.
issues.legal_principle: The court declined to decide disputed factual and legal contentions in the constitutional writ and permitted the petitioner to pursue them before the High Court. The judgment did not resolve the substantive validity of the challenged direction or the related acquisition issues.

predicates.constitutional_writ_challenges_later_adm: A petitioner brings a constitutional writ challenging an administrative direction made after an earlier judgment.
predicates.material_contentions_remain_unresolved: The petition raises factual or legal contentions that the court leaves undecided on their merits.

issues.definition: When a constitutional writ challenges a later administrative direction and material contentions remain undecided, the writ may be dismissed while the petitioner is allowed to raise those contentions before the High Court.

issues.legal_issue: A pending review application cannot be bypassed by filing a separate application for recall that raises the same review grounds and seeks an open-court hearing.
material_facts: A review application by the applicant remained pending and had not yet been considered through circulation.
The applicant separately filed an application for recall raising substantially the same issues as the pending review application.
The recall application sought an open-court hearing and included documents offered in support of the same requested relief.
issues.conclusion: The recall application was rejected as an attempt to bypass the review procedure, but the applicant was permitted to ask the Registry to list the pending review application in circulation and could submit the documents in that review application.
issues.legal_principle: Order XL Rule 3 of the Supreme Court Rules, 1966 requires a review application to be disposed of by circulation unless the Court orders otherwise. An application that is in substance a review cannot be used to obtain an oral hearing or to dispose of a pending review application indirectly.

predicates.review_application_pending: The applicant has a review application in the same matter that has not yet been disposed of.
predicates.separate_recall_application_raises_same_: The applicant filed a separate recall application that substantially repeats the issues raised in the pending review.
predicates.recall_application_seeks_open_court_hear: The recall application seeks an oral hearing outside the ordinary review procedure.

issues.definition: When a review is pending and a separate recall application repeats its issues to obtain an open-court hearing, the recall application is rejected while the pending review remains available for consideration in circulation.
